n: The topic of this lecture is the forensic medical examination of physical evidence. In solving murders, rapes and other serious crimes, the importance of this examination is very great. The plan is as follows: first the concept of physical evidence, then blood, semen, other secretions and hair examination are considered. Next we move on to forensic histological, medico-criminalistic, forensic chemical and DNA examinations. This examination is not assigned to clinical physicians. But sometimes they are involved in inspecting the scene, finding evidence and taking samples.

Now the concept of physical evidence. According to Article 203 of the Criminal Procedure Code, physical evidence is an object with physical features and properties that serve to establish the circumstances of a case. These features make it possible to establish the origin of an object, to whom it belongs, its use or suitability, its displacement and the action of substances. Physical evidence consists mainly of instruments of crime, objects that have preserved traces of the crime, and objects that were the target of criminal acts. Objects that serve to reveal a crime, to find the culprit, to refute the charge or to mitigate guilt are also evidence.

Biological material includes tissue fragments, blood, secretions, stains and hair. Secretions means saliva, urine, sweat, semen and faeces. The examination is carried out in specially equipped laboratories by trained specialists. The laboratory consists of several departments: in the forensic biology department, blood and semen stains are examined; in the forensic histology department, pieces of organs and tissues; in the medico-criminalistic department, traces of injury and weapons; and in the forensic chemistry department, toxic substances. In solving murders, rapes and other serious crimes, these examinations are of great importance.

t: The physician's role at the scene
n: Forensic medical examination of physical evidence is not assigned to clinical physicians. Such examinations are carried out by specially trained specialists in the laboratories of forensic medical institutions. In some cases general practitioners and other physicians may be involved in inspecting the scene. Note: the physician finds the evidence, describes it and takes a sample, but does not examine it. Under the law, the collection of bloodstains is carried out by the investigator. That is, the physician does not carry out the laboratory examination.

Types of bloodstains. The type of stain depends on the material on which the blood fell and on how the stain was formed. On a poorly absorbent material, a large quantity of blood forms a pool. On a material that absorbs moisture well, a soaked stain remains. Blood running down an inclined surface leaves a run. Spatter is formed by a sharp swing of an object, a blow, or when blood spurts from a large artery. Attention: a smear is formed by sliding, while an impression is formed by contact without sliding. The shape of the impression corresponds to the surface of the object.

Blood-drop traces indicate height and direction. The narrow end of a pear-shaped stain faces the direction of movement or the lower side of the surface. When blood falls from a great height, from a moving object or onto an inclined surface, the spatters also lie on this side. On a horizontal surface, a drop falling from a height of up to 10-15 cm gives a round stain with smooth edges. When it falls from higher, the edges become finely serrated, and from higher still, secondary spatters appear around it. Attention: a round stain indicates a horizontal surface and a low height, while a pear-shaped stain indicates a moving object or an inclined surface.

The following is observed when submitting bloodstains for examination. Attention: new gauze or bandage is not used, because the dressing in them adversely affects serological reactions. A control is taken for every sample: an uncontaminated area, clean gauze, or clean snow and soil. Gauze samples are dried in a place without sunlight, away from a heater, and wrapped in separate paper. Clothing, footwear and pillowcases are taken whole. From tapestry, rugs and mattresses a stained piece and a clean piece are cut out. From a hard surface such as a wall or furniture, a scraping is taken with a scalpel, or a gauze wash. Snow is melted, and soil is taken in a thick layer.

t: Sequence of questions in blood examination
n: The questions of blood examination are resolved in a strict sequence. First, whether blood is present is established. Second, whether it is human or animal, that is, species origin is resolved. Third, group origin is determined by the ABO and other systems. Fourth, to whom exactly the blood belongs is established. The examination is carried out in the forensic biology department. Sometimes sex, regional origin and origin from a pregnant woman or a woman who has recently given birth are also requested. Attention: presumptive tests only allow the presence of blood to be suspected; they do not prove it conclusively.

t: Case analysis: bloodstains at the scene
n: Now a case analysis. At the scene, clothing with bloodstains and a dry bloodstain on a wall have been found. How are samples taken? The clothing, as a small item, is taken whole. From the wall, a scraping is taken with a clean scalpel and wrapped in clean paper. For control, a similar scraping is taken from an uncontaminated area of the wall. Now ask yourself: why is a control sample needed, and where is it taken from? Try to find the answer in what has been said above.

Quick questions on bloodstains. First question: what stain does a drop falling onto a horizontal surface from a height of 10-15 cm produce? Answer: round, with smooth edges. On an inclined surface the stain will be pear-shaped. Second question: how does the stain change as the height of fall increases? Answer: the edges become serrated, and at a still greater height secondary stains, that is, spatters, appear around it. Attention, risk of error: a smear is not an impression. A smear remains when a bloodied object slides over a hard surface, while an impression remains on contact without sliding and corresponds to the surface of the object. Third question: why is a control sample needed? From a large object, a piece is taken from the stained area and from an uncontaminated area, that is, the control. A small object is taken whole.

Presumptive methods of detecting blood are used at the initial stage to select stains suspicious for blood and to make the examination targeted. With 3% hydrogen peroxide, white foam forms; this depends on the enzymes peroxidase and catalase. Benzidine with peroxide gives a blue colour, because oxygen oxidises benzidine. Phenolphthalein with peroxide gives a pinkish colour within 10-15 seconds; a change after 1 minute is disregarded. Luminol is used in a dark room and gives a light-blue glow for up to 1 minute. In ultraviolet light a bloodstain does not luminesce but appears dark brown; in an old stain, fiery-red fluorescence is seen. Attention: the tests are non-specific and may give false positives. They do not prove blood; they only allow it to be suspected.

There are four reliable methods of proving the presence of blood. The microscopic method is based on finding erythrocytes, but its scope is limited because the appearance of blood cells changes quickly. Microcrystalline methods, that is, Teichmann and Takayama, are based on crystals of haemoglobin derivatives. Because of low sensitivity they are not used in practice. The spectral method is based on the absorption of certain wavelengths by haemoglobin and its derivatives and is carried out on a microscope with a microspectral attachment. At present blood is mainly identified by the chromatographic method: thin-layer chromatography is used, on paper or on a Silufol plate.

Why is the species origin of blood determined? A bloodstain may belong to a human or to an animal. In the Chistovich-Ulengut reaction, a precipitation ring appears in a test tube to which serum against human protein has been added. If the amount of blood in the extract is small, cellulose acetate electrophoresis is appropriate. If the extract is turbid, the Ouchterlony method in agar gel is used. The ABAcard test shows both the presence of blood and its human origin at the same time.

t: Group origin of blood (ABO and other systems)
n: The group origin of blood is determined by examining various systems with group properties. The antigens and their complexes number more than several hundred thousand. Erythrocyte systems include ABO, Rhesus, MNSs and Lewis. Serum systems are Gm, Hp and Gc; in addition there are enzyme systems and the leucocyte HLA system. The examination usually begins with the ABO system. Attention: in the clinic only agglutinogens are studied, whereas in forensic medicine agglutinogens and agglutinins are studied together. In liquid blood the Schiff method is used. In a stain, agglutinogens are determined by absorption-elution and other reactions; with a small quantity, absorption-elution is recommended.

t: Attribution to a specific person and DNA
n: How is attribution to a specific person established? To find out whether a bloodstain belongs to a particular person, the trace from the scene is compared with that person's blood by group systems. The comparison begins with the ABO system, and if necessary the antigens of other systems are also examined. Two persons cannot have completely matching antigens across all group systems. However, such a comparison demands much labour and time. In recent times, the attribution of blood to a specific person has been conclusively established by DNA, that is, deoxyribonucleic acid, examination.

t: Sex, region and pregnancy signs in blood
n: In a bloodstain, signs of sex, region and pregnancy are also studied. Sex is determined by X- and Y-chromatin or by DNA examination. Y-chromatin is stained with acriquine and is characteristic only of humans. X-chromatin is found in women's cells with azure-eosin. For the question of region, epithelial cells of the area are sought, that is, cells of the nose, lung, intestine, uterus or vagina. In menstrual blood enzyme activity is higher, but this sign is not sufficiently reliable. In pregnancy, chorionic gonadotropin and oxytocinase are examined. Attention: pregnancy cannot be conclusively established from a bloodstain.

t: Newborn blood, age of stain and quantity of blood
n: In fresh stains, the blood of adults and of newborns can be distinguished by the type of haemoglobin. Adult haemoglobin, that is, HbA, is less resistant to alkali. In newborns, fetal haemoglobin, that is, HbF, is more resistant to alkali; at birth it reaches 80%, and by the end of the 1st year, 5%. But in a stain 15-20 days old this difference cannot be established. The age of a stain is determined only approximately. In calculating the quantity of blood, it is assumed that 1 litre of liquid blood leaves on average 210 g of dry residue.

t: Case analysis: questions in bloodstain examination
n: Case analysis. A stain resembling blood has been found on clothing from the scene. First the presence of blood is established, then species, group and attribution to a person. At first presumptive tests are used: benzidine, hydrogen peroxide, luminol. They give only a suspicion, not strict proof. The presence of blood is reliably confirmed by chromatography. Species origin is resolved by the Chistovich-Ulengut precipitation reaction. Question: does the stain belong to a human or an animal? How is attribution to a person resolved with the ABO group system and DNA examination? Try to answer yourself.

Finding and collecting semen traces. Semen traces may be on objects, bedding, and the victim's clothing and body; they are sought by eye or with a magnifying glass. On absorbent fabric the edges of the stain are map-like. On a hard surface a whitish-grey shiny coating is seen, and with an admixture of blood a pink or reddish colour appears. Suspect clothing and sheets are taken whole; from large material a stained piece and a control sample are taken. From the body an impression is made on X-ray film. In rape and sodomy a sample is taken with a gauze swab, and a control swab is also taken. Blood and saliva are taken from the suspect and the victim.

t: Questions in semen examination and presumptive methods
n: In semen examination, 4 questions are resolved: the presence of semen, species origin, group origin and attribution to a specific person. There are several presumptive methods. Potato juice agglutinates erythrocytes, while semen inhibits this property, that is, agglutination is inhibited. In ultraviolet light, light-blue fluorescence is seen, but this too is a presumptive method. Attention: artificial fabrics themselves may give similar fluorescence in ultraviolet light. The Florence and Barberio methods are based on a microcrystalline reaction but have no practical significance.

Reliable detection of semen relies on the morphological method. The stain is taken for examination and the morphological method is applied. If even one whole spermatozoon, that is, head, body and tail, is found, the result is positive and the presence of semen is considered proven. If the head, body or tail of a spermatozoon is found separately, this is not counted. In azoospermia and necrospermia there are no spermatozoa. In that case chromatography is used: if choline, spermine and acid phosphatase are found together, semen is considered present.

t: Species and group origin of semen; secretors
n: The group origin of semen, like that of blood, is determined by group factors, most often in the ABO system. In about 80% of people, group antigens are also found in semen and other secretions; such people are called secretors. In the Lewis system, group Le a- b+ is a secretor and group Le a+ b- is a non-secretor. In group Le a- b- secretor status cannot be clearly determined. Therefore blood and saliva samples are taken from the suspect and the victim and submitted for examination.

t: Case analysis: biological traces in a sexual crime
n: Case analysis. Rape is suspected. A sample has been taken from the vaginal area with a gauze swab, and the victim's clothing has a suspicious stain. The gauze swab is dried and wrapped in paper, and a control swab is also taken. The clothing is submitted for examination whole. Blood and saliva are taken from the suspect. Question: why are the same samples also taken from the victim? Hint: the stain may contain the victim's blood and vaginal secretions, and the group factor found may possibly belong to her.

Quick questions on semen and blood. First question: do the benzidine, hydrogen peroxide and luminol tests conclusively prove the presence of blood in a stain? Second question: what morphological criterion reliably proves the presence of semen in a stain? Third question: why is the morphological method unsuitable in azoospermia and necrospermia, and which method is used? Fourth question: which Lewis group is characteristic of secretors, and by which systems is secretor status tested? Answer each question on the basis of the slides you have covered.

t: Saliva, sweat, urine, faeces and organ fragments
n: Detecting other secretions. The sample is dried at room temperature, without sunlight, away from heat and insects; each object is wrapped separately. Attention: the object of examination and the control sample are not placed in one package. In saliva, the enzyme amylase is detected, species is established with serum, and group by ABO. In sweat, the amino acid serine is detected; species and group in the same way. In urine, creatinine and urea are found; species is not determined, and group is determined by ABO. In faeces, microscopy shows food and helminths; neither species nor group is determined. In an organ fragment, the organ is determined histologically, species by serum, group by ABO, and sex cytologically.

t: Hair examination: collection and questions resolved
n: Hair examination. Hair is found in good light by eye or with a magnifying glass. It is taken by hand or with forceps with rubber tips, without damaging it. Hairs from each area are marked and placed in a separate paper packet or envelope and sent to the laboratory. A control sample is taken from 5 areas of the head: forehead, crown, two temples and nape. From each, 20-30 hairs are cut close to the skin. The examination resolves 7 questions: whether the fibre is hair; whether it is human; its group; its region; whether it was shed or pulled out; what action was applied; and to whom it belongs.

t: Difference between human and animal hair
n: The difference between human and animal hair. A hair is divided into root and shaft; in the shaft the cuticle, cortex and medulla layers are distinguished. In human hair the cuticle is finely serrated and close-fitting, and on an impression, closely spaced wavy lines are seen. The cortex is broad, the medulla thin and interrupted, and the pigment lies at the edge of the cortex. In animal hair the cuticle is coarsely serrated, sometimes saw-like; on an impression, lines of various shapes are seen. The medulla occupies the main part of the thickness, and the pigment lies nearer the medulla. Which animal a hair belongs to is determined by comparison with a collection or atlas. If human hair is established, group and regional origin are examined next.

t: Regional origin of hair and traces of action
n: Regional origin of hair and traces of action. In determining regional origin, attention is paid to the length, thickness and cross-sectional shape of the hair. Scalp hair is up to 0.1 mm thick, with a round or oval cross-section. Eyebrows and eyelashes are 0.11-0.12 mm. Beard and moustache are 0.15-0.17 mm, with a triangular, quadrangular or polygonal cross-section. Axillary and pubic hairs give an elongated-oval or bean-shaped cross-section. The tip of a hair cut by a sharp object is smooth or finely serrated. When torn quickly the surface is smooth, and when torn slowly it is stepped. A pulled-out hair has a loop-shaped bulb on the root, while the root of a shed hair is oval or flask-shaped.

t: Case analysis: hair in a road traffic accident
n: Case analysis. After a road traffic accident, a hair has been found on the outside of a car. It is sought with a magnifying glass or by eye and taken by hand or with rubber-tipped forceps. First, under the microscope, it is resolved that this is a hair fibre, then whether it is human or animal: in human hair the cuticle scales are small and dense and the medulla is thin. In human hair, group is determined by absorption-elution in the ABO system, and region by length, thickness and cross-sectional shape. Attribution to a person is established by comparison with control samples. Attention: the result is not conclusive and is given in probabilistic form. Question: why?

t: Forensic histological examinations and diatom plankton
n: Forensic histological examinations and diatom plankton. In all cases where a post-mortem examination has been carried out, pieces of internal organs and tissues are taken for histology. Blocks and sections are prepared from them, stained with haematoxylin-eosin and examined under the microscope. Then a report is drawn up and the material is handed over to the archive. Diatom plankton makes it possible to establish whether a person entered the water alive or dead. A water sample from the body of water where the corpse was found is also submitted. Archive periods: formalin material is kept for at least 2 years; slides, blocks and the mineralisate of diatom plankton are kept for at least 3 years.

The rules of forensic histological examination. In all cases where a post-mortem examination has been carried out, pieces of internal organs and tissues must be taken for histology. Putrefaction and other post-mortem changes cannot be a ground for refusing the examination. In all cases sections are stained with haematoxylin-eosin; where necessary, selective staining and frozen sections are used. As special methods, luminescence microscopy, phase contrast and polarised light are used. The report consists of an introduction, the examination, the forensic histological diagnosis and the conclusion. If a particularly dangerous infection is found, the head is notified urgently.

Medico-criminalistic examinations. This examination is carried out in the medico-criminalistic department on the basis of a decision, ruling or referral. In the department, diagnostic, identification, that is, establishing a person's identity, and situational, that is, circumstantial, tasks are carried out. The methods used: visual, examination in infrared and ultraviolet light, measurement, photography, radiography, modelling and reconstruction. The result is issued as a conclusion or report. The document consists of an introduction, an examination and a final part; photographs, diagrams and graphs are given in the appendix.

There are five kinds of medico-criminalistic examination. In traceological examination, the injuring factor is established from the injury or trace. Ballistic examination studies firearm injuries and explosions: range of fire, entrance and exit wounds, direction of the wound track and type of weapon are determined. Identification examination establishes the identity of an unidentified corpse or bone. From skeletal remains, species, sex, approximate age, stature, injuries and their age are determined. Micrological examination studies microtraces and microparticles. In situational examination, the possibility of performing an action in the presumed conditions is studied.

Traceological and ballistic examinations. The main aim of traceological examination is to establish the injuring factor from the injury or traces. First the injury and the presumed weapon or its model are studied separately, then they are compared. The identity of the weapon is thereby established. In ballistics, the number of injuries, the sequence of shots, the entrance and exit wounds, the direction of the wound track and the firing distance are determined. In blast trauma, the mechanism of injury, the explosive device and the characteristics of the explosive substance are studied.

Identification examination is carried out to establish whether a corpse or remains of an unidentified person belong to a specific individual. First the features are studied separately, then compared, and finally a conclusion is drawn on whether identity exists. From skeletal remains, species origin, number of bodies, race, sex, approximate age and stature in life are determined. In addition, signs of disease, bodily injuries and their nature and age of infliction, and features of the verbal portrait, that is, individual features, are studied.

t: Case analysis: unidentified corpse and injury trace
n: Case analysis. A training scenario: skeletal remains of an unidentified person have been found, and an injury trace must be compared with a suspected weapon. Question: which examinations are ordered? For the bones, identification; for the injury and weapon trace, traceological examination. In identification examination the features are first studied separately, then compared, and a conclusion on identity is drawn. Attention: traceological examination establishes the identity of the injury and the weapon, whereas identification examination establishes the identity of the corpse. Do not confuse the two.

Forensic chemical and DNA examinations. Forensic chemistry detects toxic substances and determines their quantity. In each case at least two methods of different principle are recommended. An archived biological object in alcohol is kept in a refrigerator for up to one year. For ethyl alcohol, blood and urine are kept for 30 days. The DNA, that is, deoxyribonucleic acid, method is based on determining the genetic characteristics of each person. History: in 1985 minisatellite markers were identified and the potential of DNA in physical evidence was shown, and in 1986 genetic methods were introduced. The method is also called genome fingerprinting or DNA analysis.

Forensic chemical examination confirms or excludes the presence of toxic substances or their derivatives in biological objects. Preliminary methods include colour reactions, thin-layer chromatography and enzyme immunoassay. Confirmatory methods: visible, UV and IR spectroscopy, atomic absorption spectrophotometry, gas-liquid chromatography, HPLC and chromatography-mass spectrometry. Where possible, at least two methods based on different physical and chemical principles are used.

Conclusions and typical mistakes. Presumptive tests, that is, benzidine, luminol and others, are non-specific. They only allow the presence of blood to be suspected; the reliable method is chromatography. Attention, risk of error: a presumptive method is not a reliable method. A positive presumptive test does not conclusively prove the presence of blood. When taking samples, the control is taken from an uncontaminated area. The object and control must not be in one package; new gauze and bandage are not recommended. Attribution of blood to a specific person is in recent times conclusively established by DNA. In forensic chemistry the sample must be sufficient and be left for the archive.
